title: Transient Demand Hedge: soft-reserve slots and cooperative latency-aware shedder for Dedicated
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Problem: Dedicated GPU fleets must provide short-term throughput guarantees while absorbing multi-tenant bursty traffic (heterogeneous model sizes, variable request lengths) and interacting with autoscalers that take 30–120s to add capacity. Current admission is purely rate-based and global, which causes either excessive shedding of latency-sensitive tenants or sudden overloads while autoscalers spin up.

Proposal: Implement a Transient Demand Hedge (TDH) that combines three orthogonal controls: (1) soft-reserve slots (time-limited capacity tokens) that allow tenants to temporarily exceed steady-state quotas; (2) a cooperative latency-aware shedder that scores and picks excess requests to shed based on SLA weight, recent p95 contribution, and model cost; (3) standby micro-pools and autoscaler hinting to reduce cold-starts for proxied capacity.

High-level flow: 
- Ingress checks tenant steady quota (token-bucket) first. If tokens exhausted, the request attempts to acquire a soft-reserve slot from the TDH pool. Soft-reserve slots are allocated per-fleet as short-lived leases (configurable TTL, e.g., 60s).
- When soft-reserve pool full, cooperative shedder scores inflight/queued requests and drops the least valuable per scoring policy. Scoring uses: SLA weight (config), recent latency delta (p95 above target), model compute-cost estimate (tokens/sec cost), and tenant fairness history (to avoid repeated penalization).
- Standby micro-pools: a small set of prewarmed workers kept warm (fast-path) based on forecasted short-term demand (exponential smoothing over per-tenant burst metrics). Autoscaler receives hint metrics (hedge_utilization, predicted_burst_seconds) to pre-provision ephemeral capacity with lower latency.

Config surface (proposed fields): 
- tdh.enabled: bool
- tdh.pool_size: integer (absolute or percent of fleet)
- tdh.slot_ttl_s: integer
- tdh.shedder_policy: string (latency_weighted | cost_weighted | sla_first)
- tdh.standby.pool_min: integer
- tdh.autoscaler_hint_window_s: integer
- tdh.fairness_decay_s: integer

Trade-offs and rationale: 
- Soft-reserve slots are intentionally conservative (short TTL) to avoid starving other tenants long-term; they prioritize short bursts where autoscaler hasn't reacted.
- The cooperative shedder gives us nuanced control vs blunt global token-bucket drops; it requires continuous telemetry (p95 per-tenant), which increases observability costs.
- Standby micro-pools reduce tail latency for bursts but increase idle GPU minutes: we mitigate via small default sizes and autoscaler hints to bulk up only when forecasts cross thresholds.

Rollout plan: 
1) Implement feature flags and a config-only dry-run that produces scoring decisions but does not actually drop requests (2 weeks).
2) Canary with internal tenants on a single EU-dedicated zone; enable soft-reserve with tiny pool_size=2% and monitor latency, failed requests (3 weeks).
3) Gradually increase pool_size and enable standby micro-pools + autoscaler hinting in staged regions (4 weeks).
4) Add adaptive autoscaler tuning (close loop) and default policy adjustments after 2 months of telemetry.

Metrics to track: 
- per-tenant served-throughput vs guaranteed-throughput
- soft-reserve acquisition rate and eviction rate
- shedder drop rate and correctness (what we would have dropped in dry-run)
- p50/p95/p99 latency before/after for both hedged and non-hedged tenants
- autoscaler reaction time with/without hinting

Acceptance criteria: 
- No increase in sustained error-rate for SLO-tier tenants after enabling TDH at pool_size <= 5% (canary)
- Autoscaler react time for hedged bursts decreases by >= 25% with hinting enabled
- Overall token cost overhead of standby micro-pools < 3% at default config

Backward compatibility: TDH is opt-in per-fleet. Default behavior remains current admission controls when disabled. Configs can be specified at tenant-level and fleet-level; tenant-level overrides fleet-level for emergency settings.
